title: VPC/on-prem commissioning: anti-entropy TF procedures and rotation runbook (field notes)
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, pragmatic runbook capturing the field notes and procedural steps we use when commissioning private control planes in VPC and on-prem environments. Focus areas: terraform module pinning and upgrades, anti-entropy/drift detection and remediation, controlled node rotations (scale and kernel/containerd/driver updates), and KMS/secret rotation during maintenance windows. This doc is intentionally operational — checklists, commands, and quick verification steps.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: operators, SREs, platform engineers doing first-time commissions and upgrades for customer private control planes.
- Scope: control-plane components (control-plane VMs/instances, etcd, API servers, controller-manager, networking CNI hooks, ingress layer) and the Terraform/Ansible orchestration that creates them. Not a full app-level deployment runbook.

High-level approach (TL;DR):
1) Pin TF modules & provider versions; run local plan + CI plan and share plan output with on-call.
2) Run anti-entropy diff (terraform plan + kube-state checks); mark drift items with severity.
3) Schedule maintenance window; inform customer and internal SRE channel.
4) Execute rolling control-plane upgrades/rotations in single-availability-zone order; verify etcd health and API responsiveness after each step.
5) Post-ops smoke tests and rollback if any critical failures.

Quick preflight checklist (15 minutes):
- Confirm maintenance window and communicated pager/escalation list.
- Verify TF backend/lock (S3/Dynamo or remote backend) is healthy and latest state is accessible.
- kubeconfig: have admin kubeconfig and a local copy; test kubectl get nodes && kubectl get pods -A.
- etcd snapshot: take a fresh etcd snapshot and store it in customer-specified location (s3://... or NFS path).
- Snapshot Terraform state (terraform state pull > state-YYYYMMDD.tfstate).
- Confirm SSH access to nodes via bastion and that runbook user has sudo.

Terraform module strategy (practical notes):
- Always pin module tags and provider versions in root module: e.g. module.redwood_vpc.source = "git::ssh://git@.../modules/vpc.git?ref=v1.9.2" and terraform { required_providers { aws = ">= 5.0, < 6.0" } }
- Keep a small set of curated module versions in infra repo (modules-lock.json) and update in a controlled cadence (monthly for non-security, immediate for CVEs).
- For minor changes that are only param tweaks (scaling counts, tags), prefer variable-only changes to avoid module bumps in patch maintenance windows.
- Use terraform plan -out=plan.tfout and git-annex the plan output (or attach to PR) for audit.

Anti-entropy and drift detection operations:
- Run: terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -var-file=env.tfvars 
  - Exit code 0 => no change; 2 => changes present (drift or desired changes). Log plan output.
- Complement with cluster drift scan: kubectl get daemonsets, deployments, crds and run a regex/expected-checks script (scripts/cluster-drift-check.sh) to find objects changed outside TF-managed annotations.
- Classify drift: 
  - safety (e.g. missing certificates, CRD schema mismatch) => treat as high-severity.
  - cosmetic (labels, non-critical annotations) => schedule for next day.
- Remediation patterns: 
  - If Terraform-managed resource is changed, prefer to re-apply TF with careful plan. 
  - If resource was manually repaired and TF state diverges, consider terraform state replace-provider/terraform import to reconcile. Record steps in incident ticket.

Node rotation sequence (control plane VM rotation; example for a 3-az cluster):
- Do one AZ at a time. For each AZ:
  1) Get list of control-plane nodes in AZ: kubectl get nodes -l role=control-plane,zone=az1 -o wide
  2) Choose oldest node or node with most non-ready pods to rotate first.
  3) Cordon node: kubectl cordon <node>
  4) Evict control-plane pods gracefully (some pods are static; use systemctl stop static kubelet-managed pods pattern if needed).
  5) Drain if safe: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force --pod-selector="!critical"
  6) Replace instance via Terraform: update instance_count or taint + apply sequence: terraform taint module.cp.aws_instance.control_plane[0] && terraform apply -target=module.cp.aws_instance.control_plane[0] -var-file=env.tfvars
  7) Wait for node to re-register and pass kubelet health checks: kubectl get nodes; check kube-system pods status and etcd member list.
  8) Verify etcd member health: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://10.0.0.5:2379 --cacert=/etc/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/etcd/client.crt --key=/etc/etcd/client.key endpoint health
  9) Proceed to next node or next AZ.

Rotation notes and gotchas:
- If a node fails to rejoin after 10 minutes, collect journalctl -u kubelet logs and kubelet config. Consider reprovisioning with a fresh boot disk.
- Watch for kube-proxy iptables rules being stale after kernel upgrades — restart kube-proxy and network-agent daemons.
- For on-prem BMC-managed hosts, coordinate power-cycling with datacenter ops and update BMC tickets.

KMS / secret rotation during maintenance:
- When rotating KMS keys make sure to update both control plane config and any bootstrap kubeconfig secrets that reference those keys.
- Steps: 
  1) Create new key version in KMS and add as secondary key for decrypt policy.
  2) Re-encrypt secrets store (or update KMS key alias) and push to secret store (vault or S3 wrapper).
  3) Run small rollout for 1 AZ control plane to validate decryption.
  4) If successful, roll out to remaining AZs.

Upgrade plan template (48-hour window example):
- Day -2: dry-run in staging with identical TF module refs and same sequence. Collect plan outputs.
- Day -1: confirm snapshots (etcd + volumes), freeze non-essential changes, notify stakeholders.
- Day 0 (maintenance): node rotations and TF module apply; validate after each AZ. No more than one control-plane node per AZ at a time.
- Day +1: run smoke tests and increased monitoring for 72 hours.

Smoke tests and post-upgrade verification (quick):
- kubectl get cs (componentstatuses) — expect all Healthy.
- kubectl get --all-namespaces pods --field-selector=status.phase!=Running OR status.phase!=Succeeded. Expect no CrashLoopBackOff for control-plane pods.
- Run 1k synthetic requests through the ingress and measure 99th latency. Compare to baseline.
- Verify operator controllers reconcile within expected intervals (look for throttles in controller-manager logs).

Rollback decision criteria and quick rollback steps:
- Criteria to rollback: etcd quorum lost, API server unhealthy > 15 minutes, persistent pod failure impacting control plane, or automated smoke-tests failing above threshold.
- Rollback steps (fast path): 
  1) Revert Terraform changes: terraform apply -var-file=last-known-good.tfvars (we store last-known-good in S3).
  2) Restore etcd snapshot if quorum lost: etcdctl snapshot restore ... following our restore playbook.
  3) Revert KMS changes by switching alias back to previous key.
  4) Open incident and attach plan logs.

Observability & postmortem hooks (what to log during ops):
- Attach plan.tfout and the terraform apply log.
- Record etcd-member-list and etcd snapshot checksum.
- Export kubelet/journal logs for rotated nodes.
- Add a short incident note in Slack #private-ops and tag on-call.

Open questions / TODOs (for next revision):
- Automate anti-entropy remediation for low-risk label/annotation drift. 
- Add a small utility to compare TF-managed resources vs live cluster and output a reconciler suggestion file. (WIP: scripts/tf-k8s-diff).
- Verify interplay with Dedicated routing policies when performing cross-region maintenance.

Escalation contact list:
- Primary SRE: Liam O'Connor (pager)
- Backup on-call: Xiaowen Zhang
- Infra eng lead: Ruben Alvarez
- For KMS/Key issues: Security/cryptography on-call (pager)

Appendix: useful commands (copy/paste)
- Terraform plan saved: terraform plan -var-file=env.tfvars -out=plan.tfout && terraform show -json plan.tfout > plan.json
- Snapshot etcd: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints="https://127.0.0.1:2379" snapshot save /tmp/etcd-snap-$(date +%F).db --cacert=/etc/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/etcd/client.crt --key=/etc/etcd/client.key
- Taint a single instance: terraform taint module.cp.aws_instance.control_plane[1]
- Replace a provider in state (careful): terraform state replace-provider registry.terraform.io/-/old-provider registry.terraform.io/-/new-provider

Notes: these are operator field notes — prefer brevity and checkpoints over exhaustive explanation. If you take actions that diverge from this runbook, add an entry to the incident ticket with exact commands and rationale.

End of document.
